tier_reason: benchmarks-x86_64.md is generated by public criterion benches (benches/bench_compare_rgb.rs, bench_compare_rgba.rs, benches/utils/resize_functions.rs) that time fir against libvips 8.15.1, image and resize in one harness, and the page states Rust 1.97.1, the AMD Ryzen 9 5950X and the crate versions while Cargo.toml fixes the release profile (opt-level 3, LTO off). Every claimed number matches the page; the measurements are first-party but fully reproducible, so A stands.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1, cargo bench with criterion 0.7.0; Cargo.toml [profile.release] opt-level = 3, incremental = true, lto and codegen-units commented out (the image and resize crates get codegen-units = 1); no target-cpu flag; the fir rows force each CPU extension (none, SSE4.1, AVX2) through Resizer::set_cpu_extensions. libvips 8.15.1 is the Ubuntu 24.04 system library called through the libvips 1.7 Rust binding, so its build flags are the distro's.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 463 stars, 42 forks; crates.io: 20,443,908 total downloads, 4,728,314 recent (crates.io API, 2026-10-03)
corrections.caveats: Rust crate, not C++ or C: it is outside the default C++ language filter for this category and would need an FFI wrapper for C++ use. It does not compare against ImageMagick or stb_image_resize, the category's named baselines; the closest incumbent measured is libvips 8.15.1, and the RGB8 lead over it is modest (Lanczos3 13.52 ms vs 17.31 ms, about 1.28x; Bilinear 3.55 ms vs 5.58 ms, about 1.57x; derived from page data). The large margins are against the pure-Rust image and resize crates. The harness does not make libvips do identical work: libvips Box uses vips_shrink instead of a box-filter convolution; the alpha rows run libvips premultiply/unpremultiply, which produce float images (the harness casts back to the band format), so libvips resamples RGBA/LA in float while fir works in integers, which accounts for much of the RGBA8 Lanczos3 gap (332.42 ms vs 24.08 ms); and each libvips iteration builds a new pipeline and copies the result out with image_write_to_memory, while fir writes into a preallocated image with a reused Resizer, an overhead that dominates the Nearest rows. libvips runs with concurrency 1 and its cache disabled. The benchmarks are the author's own, on the author's machine. The page header says fast_image_resize 6.0.1, which is not a published crates.io version (6.0.0 and 6.1.0 are); the page was last updated on 2026-07-21 with the 6.1.0 release. The README's copy of the RGB8 table comes from an older run (libvips Lanczos3 16.07 ms vs fir AVX2 13.26 ms). The ARM64 and WASM32 benchmark pages were not opened.

notes: Numbers verified against benchmarks-x86_64.md and the harness source. The language field already reads Rust, which is correct; verify.py apply ignores the language key in corrections, so a decisions.json override is needed only if another stage set it differently. Flag the language-filter mismatch: this is a Rust entry in a C++-first category, and the libvips comparison is not like for like on the Box and alpha rows.

tier_reason: The comparison is reproducible: bench/bench.c with harness/bench_vs_upstream.sh, kernbench.sh and consumer/run.sh build upstream stb_image_resize2 v2.18 (vendored, sha256 173e6546... identical to nothings/stb master, commit 904aa67 of 2026-03-13) at -O2 against the fork's library at stated flags with clang 23.1.2 on an i7-14700F, and the CSVs are committed, so the tier stays A. The record overstated the claim: the resampler code is unchanged and the whole gain comes from build flags (upstream's own AVX2 path, -O3 and PGO against an SSE2 -O2 build), and the float rows reach only 1.12x.

corrections.baseline: stb_image_resize2.h v2.18 (nothings/stb commit 904aa67, 2026-03-13; the vendored upstream/ copy's sha256 173e654634f6ccaad98f603e686ea212eec1fe8ea6d2a5e5e8056efa10ae3880 matches nothings/stb master), compiled -O2 -ffp-contract=off for the default x86-64 (SSE2) target
corrections.claimed_speedup: results/summary.csv (upstream at -O2/SSE2 vs the fork's runtime-dispatched library at -O3 with held-out PGO, 23 rows, min ns over repeats): geomean 1.3623x (upsample 1.3495x, downsample 1.3842x); per row 1.09-1.66x: uint8 1.29-1.60x, uint16 1.52-1.66x, float 1.12-1.42x, uint8 RGBA 1.32-1.35x, RGBA_PM 1.44-1.57x, sRGB 1.12-1.22x, half 1.09-1.11x. results/kernels.csv (the same library forced to its base vs AVX2 path): geomean 1.3491x over the non-half rows, half 1.00x. results/consumer.csv (load, resize, sRGB RGBA program vs stock -O2): geomean 1.230x (1.11-1.57x). The README's +32.8% without PGO has no committed CSV. The fork's own docs/MEASUREMENT.md says upstream compiled with -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 is byte-exact and +26-34% faster by itself, so these gains are upstream's AVX2 code path enabled at runtime, not a faster resampler.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 23.1.2 (hermetic LLVM toolchain via scripts/env.sh). Baseline: upstream header with bench/bench.c at -O2 -ffp-contract=off and no -march (harness/bench_vs_upstream.sh). Fork: scripts/build_opt.sh exact compiles the unchanged header twice, lib/resize_base.c at -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 -ffp-contract=off and lib/resize_avx2.c at -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -ffp-contract=off, adds a CPUID/XGETBV dispatch layer and uses held-out PGO (PGO=1; tools/train.c trains on rows distinct from the bench rows); the bench driver is built at -O3 -march=x86-64-v2; runs are pinned with taskset -c 3.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-14700F (Raptor Lake, hybrid P/E cores), WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04
corrections.workload: bench/bench.c matrix of 23 rows (256x256 and 1024x1024 inputs; up, down and same-size; uint8/uint16/float/half/sRGB; 1ch/RGB/4ch/RGBA/RGBA_PM; default and point-sample filters; clamp edge), min ns per stbir_resize_extended call over repeats; plus an isolated base-vs-AVX2 kernel run (harness/kernbench.sh) and a downstream load-resize-sRGB consumer (harness/consumer/run.sh).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; created 2026-09-29 with 5 commits, no GitHub release (CHANGELOG lists v1.0.0)
corrections.caveats: A brand-new unofficial derivative of nothings/stb (not a GitHub fork object; 5 commits, all on 2026-09-29), not endorsed by the stb author, with no outside scrutiny. src/stb_image_resize2.h is byte-identical to upstream v2.18 (sha256 checked against nothings/stb master), and the fork adds only build glue: the same header compiled for SSE2 and for x86-64-v3 AVX2, a CPUID dispatch layer and PGO. All of the measured speedup therefore comes from build configuration, since the baseline is upstream at -O2 for the default SSE2 target. The fork's own docs/MEASUREMENT.md says upstream built with -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 is byte-exact and +26-34% faster on its own, and docs/REJECTED.md says PGO is neutral (0.9985x) on a monolithic build and only recovers the split library's layout (+32.8% to +38.0%). No head-to-head against an upstream x86-64-v3 build is published. The practical value is a portable x86-64 binary that uses upstream's AVX2 path at runtime; a project that can target x86-64-v3 gets the same speed from stock stb. Output is claimed byte-identical by harness/diff_lib.sh (8,284 checks on each of 3 dispatch paths), which is configured in CI (pass status not checked here); half-float output stays on the SSE2 path because of a signed-zero divergence. Timings come from a single WSL2 run on a hybrid P/E-core CPU, pinned to vCPU 3 with no PMU, min over repeats; the README calls per-row differences under about 3% noise. The fork documents upstream quirks it does not fix (an uninitialized read in the uint16 WRAP BOX upsample and some half filter paths; a UBSan false positive in the sRGB encoder).

notes: is_fork_of is set (it was already correct). Upstream pinning, flags and the byte-identity harness all check out, so it keeps A on reproducibility; the verdict is downgrade because the record's claim overstated what the fork contributes. The measured code does the same work as the baseline (identical source and identical output), but the baseline is built with weaker flags; the honest headline is 'stock stb's AVX2 speed in a portable binary', not a faster resizer.

tier_reason: The libvips wiki 'Speed and memory use' table is the libvips maintainers' measurement with their public vips-bench repo (gm.sh, im.sh, benchmark.sh) on a named CPU (Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04, run 12 Aug 2025). It is independent of both GraphicsMagick and ImageMagick and shows gm 1.4 at 2.05 s against ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert at 4.44 s. Both are Ubuntu packages with no compiler or flags stated, so the evidence is B, not A.

corrections.stars_or_usage: Widely packaged (Debian/Ubuntu and others); SourceForge: 3,405 downloads this week and 21 reviews, project registered 2003-02-07 (page read 2026-10-03)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ubuntu 25.04 distro packages ('systems as packaged for Ubuntu'); no compiler or flags stated; the vips-bench driver benchmark.sh sets OMP_NUM_THREADS=16, so gm and ImageMagick both ran with OpenMP threads
corrections.claimed_speedup: libvips wiki table (quickest of five runs): gm 1.4 2.05 s, 1975.81 MB peak vs ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert 4.44 s, 1499.29 MB (magick 4.41 s), about 2.2x faster (derived from page data); ppm-gm 1.58 s; jpg-gm 2.49 s vs jpg-convert 4.38 s, about 1.76x (derived from page data). gm used about 32% more peak memory than convert (derived from page data). The SourceForge page quotes a 2023 user review, 'Faster and more secure than ImageMagick' (no numbers).
corrections.workload: libvips vips-bench task: load a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 px from each edge, shrink by 10% with -filter triangle -resize 90x90%, apply a 3x3 -convolve sharpen and save; quickest real time of five runs, no disc-cache clearing. gm.sh crops after loading with -shave 100x100, while im.sh crops on load (an advantage to ImageMagick); the resize and convolve arguments are identical.
corrections.caveats: The evidence is a third-party table (the libvips project's wiki, run by the libvips maintainers with vips-bench) for one crop, shrink and sharpen task. The wiki itself says the task is file-I/O heavy with little processing, so it is not a pure resampling benchmark. GraphicsMagick 1.4 and ImageMagick 7.1.1 were Ubuntu 25.04 packages, so compiler flags and quantum-depth/HDRI settings are not stated, and both ran 16 OpenMP threads. The work is not quite identical: gm crops after a full load with -shave, while ImageMagick crops on load, which favours ImageMagick. GraphicsMagick is faster but used more peak memory (1975.81 MB vs 1499.29 MB). The project's own benchmark page (graphicsmagick.org/benchmarks.html) is unreachable here. The license is an MIT-style license; Copyright.txt also lists permissive licenses for inherited components (ImageMagick, du Pont, libtiff-derived code).

notes: The measurement belongs to the libvips maintainers (wiki page edited 2026-04-12, tests last run 12 Aug 2025), not to GraphicsMagick or ImageMagick; all the numbers belong to the gm, ppm-gm, jpg-gm, convert and jpg-convert rows. last_commit is set from the primary Mercurial repo on SourceForge (commit 779423 by Bob Friesenhahn, 2026-10-03 20:33:53), so maintenance_status stays active.
